title: Lambda executes events in replaceable environments

sections.heading: Start from an event
sections.text: A trigger supplies an event to a handler. Lambda initializes a compatible runtime, invokes your code and may reuse the environment for later work.

sections.heading: Externalize durable state
sections.text: Keep authoritative data in a suitable database or object store. Reused memory and temporary files can improve efficiency, but they are not a durable session store.

sections.heading: Separate responsibilities
sections.text: AWS operates the managed platform. You own code, dependencies, permissions, input validation, idempotency and downstream capacity.

remember: Environment reuse is an optimization, not a state guarantee.
diagram: EventBridge -> Lambda execution environment containing Init and Invoke(handler). Independent handler branch -> external durable DynamoDB/S3. Separate dashed reuse loop back to handler, labelled possible/not guaranteed; no reuse router box.

title: A Lambda image must follow the Lambda runtime contract

sections.heading: Choose a supported runtime
sections.text: Managed runtime families include Node.js, Python, Java, .NET and Ruby; supported versions change. Custom runtimes can use the Runtime API for languages such as Go or Rust.

sections.heading: Package deliberately
sections.text: ZIP deployments and compatible container images have different packaging paths. A container image still needs the Lambda Runtime API and compatible architecture/operating system.

sections.heading: Use the right compute
sections.text: ECS or Fargate can suit an arbitrary long-running container. A generic Docker image is not automatically a Lambda function; keep dependencies patched.

remember: Container packaging does not remove the runtime contract.
diagram: Compare ZIP + managed runtime and compatible ECR image + Runtime API feeding Lambda; arbitrary server container branches to ECS/Fargate.

title: Memory changes CPU allocation and execution economics

sections.heading: Tune measured demand
sections.text: For standard Event Functions, memory is configurable from 128 to 10,240 MB. CPU allocation increases with memory; 1,769 MB gives the equivalent of one vCPU, not two.

sections.heading: Bound execution time
sections.text: A standard invocation can run up to 900 seconds. Set a timeout that fits the caller and downstream system; a longer Lambda timeout does not extend an API integration automatically.

sections.heading: Treat temporary storage separately
sections.text: Configurable /tmp storage spans 512 to 10,240 MB. It is temporary environment storage; do not confuse it with function memory or a durable database.

remember: Benchmark duration and cost together; more memory can finish sooner.
diagram: Memory slider -> proportional CPU; separate /tmp disk slider; caller timeout and Lambda timeout shown as independent clocks. Visibly correct one-vCPU value.

title: Check every package and payload boundary in the path

sections.heading: Deploy within package limits
sections.text: ZIP direct upload is limited to 50 MB compressed; uncompressed code plus layers is limited to 250 MB. A compatible container image can be up to 10 GB uncompressed.

sections.heading: Distinguish invocation modes
sections.text: Standard buffered synchronous requests and responses allow 6 MB each; asynchronous invocation payloads allow 1 MB. Streamed responses use a separate supported contract.

sections.heading: Design for the smallest gate
sections.text: A front door, event producer or destination may impose a smaller limit. Put large objects in S3 and pass a scoped reference when the full chain cannot carry the data.

remember: The smallest compatible limit controls the end-to-end design.
diagram: API -> Lambda -> destination with different size gates; separate S3 large object and small reference; do not imply API 10 MB passes through 6 MB Lambda.

title: Concurrency protects both shared capacity and dependencies

sections.heading: Estimate in-flight work
sections.text: Concurrency is the number of simultaneous invocations. For a steady example, 200 requests per second times 0.5 seconds average duration requires about 100 concurrent executions.

sections.heading: Isolate critical capacity
sections.text: Reserved concurrency reserves a function share and caps its maximum. It can protect another function from a noisy neighbor and limit pressure on a database.

sections.heading: Handle throttling
sections.text: The usual regional account default is 1,000, with new-account reductions and approved increases possible. Observe throttles, retry with backoff where appropriate and respect scaling rates.

remember: Reserved capacity is not a pre-initialized environment.
diagram: Shared pool split into reserved critical function and unreserved functions; noisy stream blocked at cap before database. Equation 200 x 0.5 = 100.

title: Reserved concurrency, provisioned concurrency and SnapStart differ

sections.heading: Reserve a share
sections.text: Reserved concurrency controls capacity allocation and the function ceiling. It does not run initialization ahead of an invocation.

sections.heading: Pre-initialize for latency
sections.text: Provisioned concurrency maintains ready environments for a qualified version or alias and adds charges. Requests beyond it may use on-demand capacity if other limits allow.

sections.heading: Restore supported snapshots
sections.text: SnapStart reduces initialization for supported runtimes/configurations. Validate compatibility and restore-time uniqueness; it cannot be combined with provisioned concurrency.

remember: Choose capacity isolation separately from startup-latency optimization.
diagram: Three labeled columns: reserved slots, ready environments, snapshot restore. Separate capacity versus latency labels; no combined SnapStart + provisioned configuration.

title: A published version and an alias support safer traffic shifts

sections.heading: Freeze a release
sections.text: Publish an immutable function version after validating code and configuration. An alias provides a stable qualified name pointing to a selected release.

sections.heading: Shift traffic deliberately
sections.text: CodeDeploy can automate all-at-once, linear or canary shifts between versions. SAM can define the function, deployment preferences and required infrastructure.

sections.heading: Watch and roll back
sections.text: Use pre/post traffic hooks and CloudWatch alarms to validate health. A traffic shift is a deployment control, not proof that new code preserves data compatibility.

remember: Use versioned releases, measured traffic shifts and a tested rollback.
diagram: Alias -> v1 90% and v2 10%, CodeDeploy timeline then alarm branch rollback; label percentages sum100. SAM configuration separate from runtime request path.

title: Logs, metrics and traces explain different failure layers

sections.heading: Capture execution evidence
sections.text: The execution role needs supported CloudWatch Logs permissions. Correlate structured logs with request identifiers and protect secrets and personal data.

sections.heading: Measure symptoms
sections.text: Inspect invocations, errors, duration, throttles and concurrency. Add initialization and downstream latency evidence before changing memory or capacity.

sections.heading: Trace with current tooling
sections.text: Use supported Lambda/X-Ray tracing permissions and instrumentation. X-Ray SDKs/daemon entered maintenance in February 2026; prefer current OpenTelemetry instrumentation guidance.

remember: A trace, a log and a metric answer different questions.
diagram: Lambda connected to three distinct evidence panels: Logs(request id), Metrics(duration/errors), Trace(downstream segments). Current OpenTelemetry -> X-Ray, not false service retirement.

title: VPC attachment supplies a private path, not automatic internet

sections.heading: Attach for private resources
sections.text: Configure suitable VPC subnets and security groups for private RDS or other dependencies. Lambda uses service-managed networking and Hyperplane ENIs for this access.

sections.heading: Check every network gate
sections.text: Validate ENI permissions, DNS, subnet addresses, routes and security groups. Database authorization remains separate from network reachability.

sections.heading: Plan public access
sections.text: A public subnet does not give a Lambda function a public IP. Private IPv4 egress usually needs a working NAT path; supported AWS endpoints can avoid internet paths for those services.

remember: VPC connectivity, internet egress and data permissions are separate.
diagram: Lambda service -> Hyperplane ENI in private subnet -> private RDS via SG; separate route toward NAT/public endpoint. Explicit public-subnet-alone != internet badge.

title: A NAT egress path can provide a stable public IPv4 identity

sections.heading: Route from private subnets
sections.text: Send required IPv4 internet traffic from the function network path to a public NAT gateway in a suitable public subnet.

sections.heading: Complete the path
sections.text: The NAT gateway uses an Elastic IP and an internet-gateway route. External systems see the NAT egress identity; Lambda itself still has no public IPv4 address.

sections.heading: Design availability and cost
sections.text: Use deliberate AZ routing and allowlist all possible egress addresses. Include NAT processing, transfer, routing and dependency failure in the design.

remember: A fixed egress IP belongs to the NAT path, not the function.
diagram: Private subnet Lambda/ENI -> public subnet NAT(EIP) -> IGW -> external allowlist API; arrows routed correctly distinct subnet boundaries; show EIP on NAT only.

title: Synchronous invocation leaves retry decisions with the caller

sections.heading: Wait for the outcome
sections.text: A direct SDK/CLI request or API integration waits for a result within its own timeout and response contract.

sections.heading: Interpret both layers
sections.text: A successful transport response does not always mean function success. Check function error indicators or the front-door status and correlated logs.

sections.heading: Retry deliberately
sections.text: Use bounded backoff, jitter and idempotency for retryable failures. Retrying a completed write after a lost response can create duplicate side effects.

remember: A timeout can leave the business outcome uncertain.
diagram: Caller -> Lambda with response arrow returning outcome; lost-response scenario after committed DBwrite -> retry -> idempotency record prevents duplicate.

title: Asynchronous acceptance is not successful processing

sections.heading: Queue before execution
sections.text: Supported sources such as S3, SNS and EventBridge can invoke Lambda asynchronously. Acceptance places an event in Lambda-managed processing; it is not a final application result.

sections.heading: Separate retry classes
sections.text: By default, function errors get two additional attempts. Throttling and system errors follow queue retry behavior for up to six hours by default, subject to configuration and age.

sections.heading: Expect duplicates
sections.text: An event can be delivered more than once, even without a function error. Use stable event identifiers, safe writes and monitored failure retention.

remember: Three attempts describes default function errors, not every failure.
diagram: Source -> async queue(accepted) -> function attempt1,error -> retry2 -> retry3 -> failure retention; side note throttles/system errors have different age/retry path.

title: Destinations retain an outcome; a DLQ retains an event

sections.heading: Choose retained evidence
sections.text: An asynchronous destination includes an invocation record with request/response context. Configure success and failure destinations independently.

sections.heading: Know destination support
sections.text: Supported choices include standard SQS, standard SNS, Lambda and EventBridge; S3 is supported for failure records. A function DLQ uses standard SQS or SNS event content.

sections.heading: Test delivery itself
sections.text: The execution role needs destination permissions. Check size compatibility, encryption and DestinationDeliveryFailures; a failure archive is useless if delivery is denied.

remember: Successful function handling and successful failure-record delivery are separate checks.
diagram: Lambda outcome branches success destination record and failure destination record; separate DLQ originalevent panel. Annotate S3 failure-only and SNS256KB smaller-than-async.

title: A poll-based event source mapping has its own retry contract

sections.heading: Let the mapping poll
sections.text: Lambda event source mappings poll supported queues or streams such as SQS, Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams. They batch records and invoke the handler; this is not the async invocation queue.

sections.heading: Control failed records
sections.text: For SQS, align visibility, batch processing and supported partial-batch responses. For streams, checkpoints, ordering and retry/age settings affect backlog and poisoned records.

sections.heading: Protect throughput
sections.text: Tune source capacity, batch windows, concurrency and idempotency together. A queue buffers demand; it does not create infinite processing capacity.

remember: Match retries to the source integration, not just to Lambda.
diagram: SQS -> ESM poller -> Lambda handler; handler outcomes -> poller; poller deletes successful messages while failed messages remain until visibility/retry. Kinesis -> ESM checkpoint reader -> Lambda; failure retains checkpoint and retries existing records, never reinserts them.

title: A thumbnail workflow needs recursion and duplicate protection

sections.heading: Separate input and output
sections.text: Use a dedicated input prefix or bucket and a distinct thumbnail destination. Filter notifications so generated thumbnails do not trigger an endless loop.

sections.heading: Process a stable object
sections.text: Read the referenced object with scoped permissions, generate the image and write output plus useful metadata such as source identity, size and creation time.

sections.heading: Handle partial completion
sections.text: Object output and DynamoDB metadata writes are separate operations. Use deterministic keys, conditional/idempotent updates, retries and reconciliation for partial failures.

remember: An event-driven diagram still needs a consistency and recovery design.
diagram: Original branching workflow inputphotos/ -> event -> Lambda -> thumbnails/ plus DynamoDBmetadata. No output-to-trigger loop; dedup key and partialfailure checkpointlabels.

title: Scheduled invocation requires permissions and execution evidence

sections.heading: Choose a schedule
sections.text: Use a supported EventBridge Scheduler configuration for hourly, cron or one-time work. Specify the intended timezone and flexible window behavior where relevant.

sections.heading: Authorize the target
sections.text: The scheduler execution role needs permission to invoke the qualified function. Configure supported retry and failed-delivery retention settings.

sections.heading: Validate completion
sections.text: Scheduler delivery success and handler business success are different signals. Make the job idempotent and monitor function results as well as target invocation failures.

remember: A schedule firing does not prove that the job finished.
diagram: Clock schedule -> Scheduler(executionrole) -> Lambda -> completedbusinessrecord; deliveryfailure branch vs processingfailure branch clearly separated.

title: Fan-out and buffering trade latency for controlled work intake

sections.heading: Fan out notifications
sections.text: An S3 event can reach SNS and independently subscribed consumers. Each subscription needs its own delivery/security design.

sections.heading: Insert a queue intentionally
sections.text: SNS to SQS to a Lambda poller provides buffering, batching and separate consumer pacing. It adds queueing delay and new retention/retry responsibilities.

sections.heading: Keep payload semantics clear
sections.text: Raw-message delivery versus an SNS envelope changes the handler input. Handle duplicates and recover the correct business event rather than assuming identical payloads.

remember: A buffer absorbs bursts only within its retention and processing limits.
diagram: Original comparison: SNS branches two independent consumers; lower lane SNS->SQS backlog->poller->Lambda, annotate paced batches and added latency.

title: Current Lambda offerings have different execution contracts

sections.heading: Keep the standard scope
sections.text: The course core uses standard event-driven Lambda functions. Its ordinary per-invocation duration, memory and concurrency limits must be labelled with that scope.

sections.heading: Recognize supported exceptions
sections.text: Lambda Managed Instances uses supported EC2 capacity with Lambda-managed operations. Eligible asynchronous and event-source-mapping invocations can run up to 90 minutes, with source exceptions.

sections.heading: Separate durable orchestration
sections.text: Durable functions checkpoint and resume supported multi-step code; wall-clock workflow duration is not one uninterrupted invocation. Newer Lambda offerings require their own current compatibility and quota check.

remember: Do not turn a standard-function limit into a universal Lambda claim.
diagram: Three separate cards: standard event function 15-min invocation; ManagedInstances eligible90-min; durable checkpoints+wait+resume. Label supplementary current-AWS context.

title: Invocation permission differs from the function execution role

sections.heading: Authorize the caller
sections.text: The invoking principal or service must be allowed to invoke the selected function/version/alias. Scope service resource policies to the expected source where supported.

sections.heading: Authorize the code
sections.text: The execution role authorizes what handler code can do, including selected database, object, secret, logging and destination operations.

sections.heading: Protect credentials and inputs
sections.text: Use temporary credentials, scoped secret retrieval and supported encryption. Validate events and avoid leaking tokens or secret values into logs and error responses.

remember: The caller invokes; the execution role accesses dependencies.
diagram: Caller/service -> invocation permission gate -> Lambda; separate execution-role gate -> S3/DynamoDB/Secrets. Never draw callerpolicy as automatically grantingfunctiondataaccess.

title: Choose REST, HTTP or WebSocket APIs by required features

sections.heading: REST API feature depth
sections.text: Use REST API when supported requirements include usage plans/API keys, request validation, stage caching, WAF, private API endpoints or canary releases.

sections.heading: HTTP API simplicity
sections.text: HTTP APIs provide a leaner RESTful front door with supported JWT/IAM/Lambda authorization and integrations. They do not inherit every REST API feature.

sections.heading: WebSocket interaction
sections.text: WebSocket APIs keep client connections for bidirectional messages. Connection lifecycle, routes and backend callback permissions become part of the application.

remember: RESTful HTTP traffic does not identify the API Gateway product.
diagram: Three product cards REST/HTTP/WebSocket with precisefeaturebadges and websocketsbidirectionalarrows. No RESTfeaturebadges underHTTP.

title: An integration connects API requests to a compatible backend

sections.heading: Select the backend contract
sections.text: API Gateway can integrate with Lambda, supported AWS service operations or HTTP endpoints. Select proxy versus custom mapping behavior intentionally.

sections.heading: Transform and validate
sections.text: Request parameters, body formats, status responses and error mappings depend on API/integration type. Importing OpenAPI helps define the contract but does not authorize the backend.

sections.heading: Authorize and connect
sections.text: Use supported invocation permissions or integration credentials, plus network reachability for private/on-premises dependencies. Do not expose arbitrary AWS APIs without a defined allowlist.

remember: An integration is a contract, permission path and network path.
diagram: APImethod branches Lambda proxy, selectedAWSoperation, HTTPbackend; separate mapping/permission/networkgates, include onprem with validatedreachability.

title: Direct AWS integration can remove an unnecessary function hop

sections.heading: Map one supported operation
sections.text: For simple authenticated intake, a supported API integration can call an operation such as sending a message to SQS or starting a workflow.

sections.heading: Scope the integration role
sections.text: Grant the minimum target action and resource. Validate input, translate the request shape and return a suitable acceptance response.

sections.heading: Preserve business logic where needed
sections.text: Removing a pass-through function can reduce code and an invocation hop. Keep compute when custom validation, orchestration or transformation actually requires it.

remember: Less code is useful only when the integration still meets the contract.
diagram: Compare client->API->pass-throughLambda->SQS with client->API(integrationrole scoped SendMessage)->SQS. Label enqueueacceptance!=jobcomplete.

title: An API deployment stage and a Lambda alias are separate controls

sections.heading: Deploy an API configuration
sections.text: A REST API deployment captures API configuration; a named stage points to a deployment. Stage count is quota-bound, not literally unlimited.

sections.heading: Route to a function release
sections.text: The integration can invoke a qualified Lambda alias. API stage selection and alias version weighting are separate mechanisms with independent configuration.

sections.heading: Change and recover deliberately
sections.text: Use supported REST canary settings or controlled deployment changes; test permissions, stage variables, cached responses and client compatibility before rollback.

remember: API rollout and function rollout must be coordinated.
diagram: Two independentselectors APIstage->deployment and Lambdaprodalias->v1/v2; distinct knobs, no conflatingAPIcanarywithaliasweight.

title: Time and payload limits depend on API type and transfer mode

sections.heading: Check buffered constraints
sections.text: A standard REST API payload limit is 10 MB. Buffered Lambda integration has its own 6-MB request/response boundary and format overhead.

sections.heading: Qualify timeout claims
sections.text: Regional and private REST integration timeouts can be raised beyond the usual 29 seconds, potentially reducing account throttle quota. HTTP and edge-optimized APIs have different limits.

sections.heading: Recognize response streaming
sections.text: Supported REST proxy response streaming can run up to 15 minutes and exceed buffered response sizes. It does not turn large uploads into streamed requests or remove downstream limits.

remember: Label API type, integration and transfer mode before quoting a limit.
diagram: Three independentgates clientpayload, APIintegrationtimeout, Lambdabuffer; separate supportedRESTresponse-streaminglane(outboundonly).

title: Upload large objects directly with a tightly scoped S3 URL

sections.heading: Authorize the upload request
sections.text: The application asks a trusted API for upload permission. Validate user/tenant context, intended object key, expiry and allowed operation.

sections.heading: Return a limited capability
sections.text: A permitted signer creates a short-lived presigned request. The browser sends object bytes directly to S3 using the signed method and required headers.

sections.heading: Validate the stored result
sections.text: Configure S3 CORS where needed, encryption, size/checksum constraints and completion processing. A presigned URL is a bearer capability; protect it from disclosure.

remember: Issue permission through the API; send large object bytes to S3.
diagram: Numbered arrows 1browser->API permission 2API->signer 3URLreturnbrowser 4browser->S3 directly. No largeupload throughLambda/API.

title: Edge, Regional and private endpoints change the client path

sections.heading: Edge-optimized REST
sections.text: A managed CloudFront edge path fronts one regional API. Edge presence does not create independent multi-Region backends.

sections.heading: Regional endpoint
sections.text: Clients connect to a regional API endpoint; an intentionally configured CloudFront distribution can add edge behavior with explicit cache and origin settings.

sections.heading: Private REST endpoint
sections.text: Private API access uses execute-api interface endpoints and compatible private connectivity, endpoint/resource policies and API authorization.

remember: Endpoint location and backend resilience are separate decisions.
diagram: Three separate paths: managed CloudFront->regional REST, direct regional REST with optional ownCloudFront, private client->execute-api interface endpoint->service-managed private REST API. Customer VPC contains client/endpoint only; API service outside.

title: A private API combines network reachability and policy gates

sections.heading: Create a private client path
sections.text: Reach an execute-api interface endpoint through a VPC or supported connected network. Configure private DNS, subnet placement and endpoint security groups deliberately.

sections.heading: Evaluate distinct policies
sections.text: An endpoint policy and API resource policy restrict access; supported conditions include aws:SourceVpc and aws:SourceVpce. Method authorization still applies.

sections.heading: Support intentional sharing
sections.text: One endpoint can reach multiple permitted private APIs, including supported cross-account designs. Private connectivity does not make every API in the Region available.

remember: Reachability is necessary; endpoint, resource and method authorization still matter.
diagram: Privateclient -> endpointSG -> endpointpolicy -> APIresourcepolicy -> methodauth -> API. CrossaccountAPI sidecard samegates; endpointsharedmultipleallowedAPIs.

title: Private backend integration is different from a private API

sections.heading: Separate the two directions
sections.text: A public API can reach a private backend through a VPC link. A private API controls how clients reach API Gateway; the two decisions are independent.

sections.heading: Use current VPC-link support
sections.text: Current REST VPC links V2 support compatible ALB/NLB private integrations. Legacy V1 uses its own narrower contract. HTTP APIs have separate integration options.

sections.heading: Validate backend routing
sections.text: Check ownership, listener ports, security groups, TLS server name and path mapping. REST private integrations can include the stage in the backend path unless overridden.

remember: Private ingress and private backend connectivity are different features.
diagram: Internetclient->publicAPI->VPCLinkV2->privateALB->service; separate privateclient->privateAPI inset. ClearlyALBbehindVPCLink notpublicAPIitself.

title: A cache key is part of the authorization design

sections.heading: Cache compatible responses
sections.text: REST API stage caching reduces backend calls. Default TTL is 300 seconds, supported up to 3,600; TTL zero disables caching. GET caching is enabled by default when stage method caching is turned on.

sections.heading: Separate users and variants
sections.text: Select cache-key parameters that represent the actual response. Never serve one tenant’s private data to another through a shared cache key.

sections.heading: Operate the cache
sections.text: Method overrides, encryption, authorized invalidation and stage flush are separate controls. Monitor hits/misses, response size, stale data and hourly cache cost.

remember: Fast cached data is wrong if its identity or freshness boundary is wrong.
diagram: Cachelookup key(tenant+resource+variant) -> hitresponse or missbackend; two tenants separatedkeys; invalidationpermissiongate.

title: Authenticate callers with the mechanism the API supports

sections.heading: IAM and signed requests
sections.text: AWS_IAM uses SigV4-signed requests with permitted identities. It suits authorized AWS callers; do not transmit a raw secret access key as a bearer token.

sections.heading: Tokens and authorizers
sections.text: REST supports Cognito user-pool and Lambda authorizers. HTTP APIs support compatible JWT authorizers, including suitable Cognito/OIDC issuers, plus supported IAM/Lambda options.

sections.heading: Enforce application permissions
sections.text: A valid identity is not blanket access to every record. Scope authorizer caching and check tenant/resource permissions in trusted application logic.

remember: Validate identity, then authorize the requested operation and data.
diagram: IAM caller signs API request. User/client signs in with Cognito or compatible issuer, issuer returns token to client, client sends token to API. Then separate application tenant/resource authorization gate. Issuer never sends client API request.

title: Resource policies, backend roles and TLS solve different gates

sections.heading: Restrict API invocation
sections.text: A supported REST resource policy can restrict principals and network context. Explicit denies and cross-account policy requirements must be evaluated with method authorization.

sections.heading: Allow the integration
sections.text: Backend invocation needs compatible Lambda resource permission or an integration role scoped to the required AWS action. This is separate from the API caller’s data permissions.

sections.heading: Secure the endpoint
sections.text: Use compatible ACM certificates and custom-domain mappings with appropriate DNS records. Regional/edge certificate rules differ; a DNS alias is not authorization.

remember: Caller policy, integration policy and transport protection are not interchangeable.
diagram: Actual HTTPS path caller->API Gateway custom-domain TLS endpoint->integration->Lambda and response back. Route53 lookup and ACM certificate are dotted side/configuration associations. Resource/method checks inside API; backend permission is logical annotation.

title: CORS is a browser response rule, not an API access boundary

sections.heading: Recognize the browser check
sections.text: A browser compares origins and may send an OPTIONS preflight for the intended method and headers. Non-browser clients are not secured by CORS.

sections.heading: Return compatible headers
sections.text: Configure allowed origins, methods and headers on preflight and relevant actual/error responses. Credentialed requests require an explicit compatible origin, not a wildcard.

sections.heading: Keep real authorization
sections.text: IAM/token checks, tenant authorization and CSRF protections where applicable remain necessary. A browser can hide a response even though the backend already processed the request.

remember: CORS controls browser access to responses; it does not replace authorization.
diagram: Browser OPTIONS->APIpreflightthenactualrequest->responseCORSgate; separateCLIpathstillneedsauthnoCORSgate. Showbackendmayexecuteevenifbrowserblocksresponse.

title: Usage-plan keys meter clients; they do not authenticate users

sections.heading: Identify an API consumer
sections.text: REST API keys can identify developer customers across associated stages and methods. A usage plan sets supported request-rate and period quota targets.

sections.heading: Retain real authorization
sections.text: Use IAM, a Cognito user pool or a compatible authorizer to protect access. A leaked API key is not a trustworthy user or tenant identity.

sections.heading: Budget for best effort
sections.text: Usage-plan quotas and throttling are best effort, not hard spending caps. Regional/account and downstream throttles are separate; handle 429 responses with bounded backoff.

remember: API keys support metering, not secure identity or a hard cost ceiling.
diagram: APIkey->usageplanmeter alongside separateJWT/IAMauthgate thenbackend; ratebucket andmonthlyquota targetnot hardcaplabels.

title: Diagnose API errors at the layer that produced them

sections.heading: Inspect client-side failures
sections.text: 400 can indicate invalid input; 401/403 can indicate authentication, policy, WAF or other access/path issues. A 429 may come from API throttles or downstream capacity.

sections.heading: Inspect integration failures
sections.text: A 502 often indicates a failed or malformed proxy response; 503 signals unavailability; a 504 can indicate integration timeout. Status alone is not a complete root cause.

sections.heading: Correlate before retrying
sections.text: Use request identifiers, access/execution logs, integration status and Lambda metrics. Retry only suitable failures with idempotency and investigate continuing work after timeouts.

remember: An HTTP code narrows the investigation; evidence identifies the cause.
diagram: Layereddiagnosticboard client/API/integration/Lambda with400403429502504 routedtolabeledchecks; noall502=orderclaim.

title: API observability separates gateway time from backend time

sections.heading: Log the right context
sections.text: Supported access logs record request identifiers, caller context and status. REST execution logging can add integration detail; redact credentials and sensitive payloads.

sections.heading: Compare latency layers
sections.text: Gateway Latency and IntegrationLatency measure different portions of the path. Add 4XX/5XX counts, throttle signals and REST cache-hit/miss evidence.

sections.heading: Respect product differences
sections.text: REST supports execution logs, supported Firehose access-log delivery and X-Ray tracing. HTTP APIs have a leaner monitoring feature set; use current instrumentation guidance.

remember: Measure the gateway and integration separately before tuning either.
diagram: Six chronological events: API receives request, preprocessing, sends integration request, receives integration response, response processing, sends client response. Latency spans full gateway interval. IntegrationLatency spans only integration send to integration response. Separate logs/metrics/traces cards.

title: WebSocket routing handles a connection lifecycle

sections.heading: Connect and authorize
sections.text: Clients establish a wss connection. Authenticate at the supported connection gate and retain trusted user/tenant association with the connection identifier.

sections.heading: Route messages
sections.text: Use $connect, $disconnect and $default plus application routes selected from message content. Route handlers can use supported Lambda, HTTP or AWS integrations.

sections.heading: Handle connection limits
sections.text: Clients need reconnect and resubscribe behavior. Connection state in DynamoDB is an application record; disconnect delivery and cleanup still need robust handling.

remember: A persistent connection still needs lifecycle, authorization and recovery logic.
diagram: Client<->WebSocket API with connect/message/disconnect routes to handlers and trusted connectionId state. Optional configured route response/callback. Reconnect originates client->API. No automatic frame implied from handler return.

title: WebSocket callbacks use a signed HTTPS management request

sections.heading: Use the right endpoint
sections.text: Clients use wss to connect. Backend callbacks use the HTTPS @connections management endpoint for the correct API, stage/custom-domain mapping and connection identifier.

sections.heading: Authorize the backend
sections.text: Sign management requests with SigV4 and scope execute-api:ManageConnections permissions. The original client token is not an automatic backend IAM permission.

sections.heading: Handle stale connections
sections.text: A callback can fail with GoneException if the client is gone or not yet established. Remove stale state and implement reconnect/recovery without blind repeated sends.

remember: Client WebSocket traffic and backend HTTPS callbacks are different paths.
diagram: Client<->wssAPI persistentconnection; Lambda->signedHTTPSPOST /@connections/id ->API->client; DynamoDBidlookup; staleid -> Gone -> cleanup. NeverwsscallbackURL.

title: AppSync resolvers connect a GraphQL schema to data

sections.heading: Define the contract
sections.text: A GraphQL schema defines available types, fields and operations. Clients request selected fields; schema and resolver logic determine what actually runs.

sections.heading: Choose compatible data sources
sections.text: Supported resolvers can reach DynamoDB, eligible Aurora/Data API paths, OpenSearch, HTTP and Lambda-backed custom behavior. Verify the exact data-source contract.

sections.heading: Plan operation and cost
sections.text: Resolvers need scoped access and valid mapping/runtime behavior. Monitor requests, errors, latency and fan-out; asking for fewer fields does not guarantee fewer backend operations.

remember: A GraphQL schema describes data; resolvers enforce the real access path.
diagram: Clientselectedfields->AppSyncschema->3resolverbranches DynamoDB/AuroraviaDataAPI/Lambdacustom, smallerHTTP/OpenSearchsourcecards; avoidcopyingPDFfanoutcomposition.

title: AppSync caller authorization and resolver IAM are separate

sections.heading: Authenticate the caller
sections.text: Supported GraphQL modes include Cognito user pools, IAM, OIDC, Lambda and API key. Choose a suitable mode rather than treating an unauthenticated key as private user identity.

sections.heading: Authorize fields and tenants
sections.text: Cognito group rules can distinguish readers from writers. Enforce owner/tenant predicates in resolver/application logic as well as schema-level permissions.

sections.heading: Authorize the data source
sections.text: AppSync resolver roles need scoped backend IAM permissions independently of the caller token. Test negative cross-tenant and forbidden mutation cases.

remember: A valid JWT does not authorize every field or every data item.
diagram: CognitoJWTgroups reader/writer->AppSyncfieldauth->resolvertenantpredicate->separatedatasourceIAMgate->DynamoDB. Reader deniedmutation visible.

title: Subscriptions and offline synchronization require different designs

sections.heading: Push live changes
sections.text: AppSync GraphQL subscriptions use secure WebSockets and supported mutation-linked updates. Apply subscription authorization and filtering to avoid exposing another tenant’s events.

sections.heading: Recover client state
sections.text: Offline access/synchronization depends on compatible client libraries, local storage and conflict/version handling. Reconnection may require a fresh query, not just replaying a socket.

sections.heading: Distinguish the API product
sections.text: AppSync Events supplies a separate managed publish/subscribe event API. It is not the same schema/resolver contract as GraphQL subscriptions; old MQTT illustrations are not a universal current protocol.

remember: Live transport, durable history and offline conflict resolution are separate.
diagram: Mutation->GraphQLsubscription->connectedclient; offlineclientlocalcache->reconnectquery+conflictcheck; separateAppSyncEvents pub/sub card notschemamutation.

title: Choose an HTTP front door by policy, limits and operating model

sections.heading: ALB with Lambda
sections.text: An ALB can route compatible HTTP requests to Lambda targets alongside other target groups and supported WAF controls. Its event/size/response contract differs from API Gateway.

sections.heading: API Gateway or function URL
sections.text: API Gateway offers product-specific API controls. A Lambda function URL exposes a simpler HTTP endpoint with supported IAM or public access configuration; validate its own permissions and limits.

sections.heading: Choose the full path
sections.text: Compare API features, auth, network exposure, payload, latency, scaling and cost. A direct AWS integration may avoid compute; a custom HTTP backend may need private connectivity.

remember: The simplest front door is the one that still meets every requirement.

title: A regional API needs a separate regional data and recovery plan

sections.heading: Duplicate the right layers
sections.text: A multi-Region design needs compatible API deployments, function releases, identity configuration, dependencies and secrets in each intended Region.

sections.heading: Choose data behavior
sections.text: Replicate or recover data using the chosen datastore’s actual consistency and failover model. Avoid two uncontrolled writers during an incident.

sections.heading: Test traffic recovery
sections.text: Validate custom domains, certificates, routing, health checks and client DNS/reconnect behavior. An edge-optimized endpoint still has a regional API behind it.

remember: Global DNS or an edge entry point is not a complete regional recovery design.

title: Lambda walkthrough: prove asynchronous failure retention

sections.heading: Prepare the sandbox
sections.text: Use a disposable function, least-privilege execution role and supported failure destination. Set bounded retry/age values and record the test event identifier.

sections.heading: Run a controlled failure
sections.text: Submit an asynchronous test invocation. The accepted response proves intake only; inspect handler logs and configured retry behavior.

sections.heading: Verify and clean up
sections.text: Find the retained invocation record, validate its event identifier and check delivery-failure metrics. Restore normal code, remove temporary resources and confirm no unexpected invocations continue.

remember: Verify the failed-event record, not only the accepted invoke response.
diagram: Illustrative sandboxthreepanels configuration, accepted202notcomplete, failurearchiveeventidmatchinglogs. No claimactualAWSaccountwasexecuted.

title: Lambda walkthrough: isolate a private-network timeout

sections.heading: Start with evidence
sections.text: In a disposable VPC-attached function, capture the request ID and exact failed dependency. Separate a private RDS connection from a public HTTPS request.

sections.heading: Inspect the right path
sections.text: Check DNS, subnet routes, security groups, NAT/EIP/IGW or the service endpoint, plus relevant IAM and database grants. A public subnet alone is not a fix.

sections.heading: Retest and remove changes
sections.text: Make the smallest justified configuration correction and rerun the same bounded request. Confirm success with logs and dependency evidence, then remove sandbox-only rules/resources.

remember: Diagnose the actual dependency path before raising the timeout.
diagram: Illustrative private Lambda -> RDS local connection fails because RDS SG lacks TCP5432 ingress from Lambda SG. Separate public HTTPS path via NAT/IGW succeeds. Add only RDS ingress; retest and remove sandbox rule. NAT is never on the private RDS path.

title: API walkthrough: distinguish throttling from a malformed response

sections.heading: Create two controlled cases
sections.text: In a sandbox API/Lambda integration, use distinct request identifiers for a bounded throttle test and an intentionally invalid proxy-response shape.

sections.heading: Read correlated evidence
sections.text: For an API Gateway stage-throttle 429, inspect stage limits and confirm rejected requests did not invoke Lambda. For 502, inspect integration logs and the REST Lambda proxy response contract.

sections.heading: Verify the specific correction
sections.text: Apply an appropriate throttle/capacity or response-shape change, retest the same case and remove temporary settings. Preserve redacted before/after evidence.

remember: A 429 and a 502 require different evidence and different fixes.
diagram: Two illustrative REST cases: API Gateway stage throttle429 and malformed Lambda proxy response502. Correct respective stage throttle or response shape; retest and clean up.

title: AppSync walkthrough: prove allowed and denied data access

sections.heading: Define a small policy matrix
sections.text: Use a disposable schema/table and test identities: an allowed reader, an allowed writer and a different tenant. Record expected query and mutation outcomes.

sections.heading: Run positive and negative tests
sections.text: Confirm permitted reads/writes, reject reader mutations and reject cross-tenant item access. A successful token check alone does not prove the data predicate.

sections.heading: Collect safe evidence
sections.text: Record operation, trusted identity/tenant, policy version and outcome without logging raw tokens. Remove test identities, items and resources when finished.

remember: A tenant boundary is demonstrated by expected denials as well as allowed requests.
diagram: IllustrativematrixreaderqueryALLOW/readermutationDENY/tenantAcrossTenantBDENY/writerownmutationALLOW; trace callerfieldresolverdatagates.

title: Release walkthrough: measure a canary before full promotion

sections.heading: Prepare compatible versions
sections.text: Publish two sandbox function versions behind an alias and point a test API integration to that alias. Keep schema/data behavior compatible for rollback.

sections.heading: Shift a bounded share
sections.text: Use a supported deployment configuration such as a ten-percent canary. Exercise representative requests and observe errors, latency and custom correctness signals.

sections.heading: Promote or recover
sections.text: Use hooks/alarms to determine promotion or rollback. Verify the alias target and the API response after the action, then delete unused sandbox releases and settings.

remember: A successful rollout needs correctness evidence, not only a completed deployment status.

title: Optimize the complete serverless path, not one price line

sections.heading: Measure useful work
sections.text: Benchmark memory, duration, initialization and concurrency with realistic payloads. Reduce unnecessary hops or repeated data access only when the business contract remains correct.

sections.heading: Account for supporting charges
sections.text: Include API requests, Lambda capacity/duration, provisioned concurrency, NAT, logs, cache hours, data transfer and downstream database operations where applicable.

sections.heading: Keep guardrails
sections.text: Use quotas, alarms, budgets, bounded retries and failure retention. Neither automatic scaling nor usage-plan metering guarantees unlimited capacity or a hard spending ceiling.

remember: Optimize latency, reliability and total cost together.
diagram: API Gateway -> Lambda -> private RDS directly. Separate optional Lambda -> NAT -> IGW -> external HTTPS path. Cost tags and illustrative memory-duration curve, explicitly not measured data.

title: Identify who invokes Lambda and who retries the work

sections.heading: Wait for selected synchronous triggers
sections.text: API Gateway, an ALB or a direct SDK call can wait for a function result. Most Cognito user-pool triggers are synchronous; verify the selected trigger’s fixed timeout, exception and retry contract.

sections.heading: Separate push-source delivery
sections.text: S3, SNS and EventBridge can submit asynchronous events. Supported IoT rule and CloudWatch Logs subscription integrations have source-specific permission and payload contracts; source delivery and handler processing are separate.

sections.heading: Recognize poll-based processing
sections.text: SQS, Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams use supported event source mappings that poll and batch records. Their checkpoint, visibility and retry behavior differs from Lambda’s asynchronous queue.

remember: Identify the source integration before choosing timeout, retry and failure retention.
diagram: Three clearly separated groups of AWS service icons: synchronous API Gateway/ALB/Cognito with waits; push S3/SNS/EventBridge plus IoT and CloudWatch Logs source-specific integrations; poll SQS/Kinesis/DynamoDB Streams -> event source mapping -> Lambda. Never put a direct push arrow from queue to function without the poller label. Use compact service cards and a distinct retry-owner badge per group, no invented numeric limits.
